chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: Who guided her career after Claude: Lou Singer, Columbia and MCA
summary: After the break with Claude, Lou Singer arranged for her; Columbia's artists bureau ended and she moved to MCA.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Can I ask you a general question? When you ceased to be associated with Claude Thornhill, who took responsibility for your, the artistic choices that you made? You know, who was running your career for you?
Well after I sort of broke off with Claude and he was no longer working with me I got you know, I sort of got hung up with that folk song bag and I had to keep looking around for material. So I

ran into Lou Singer who, by that time had begun to do some arrangements with John Kirby, and he worked for Leeds and he did allot of transcribing up there. So he was very helpful in helping me to find material. And so I got a chance to record things like "Molly Malone", "Who Is Sylvia", and because we was using Kirby's band it sounded pretty much the same as the early arrangements. And of course, you know, "If I had Ribbon Bow", one of the songs that I did for quite a long time became quite popular. Lou wrote that himself. It was based on a very early American hillbilly song and it was quite popular, I mean, when I worked in the clubs.
It was a replacement, I suppose, for 'Loch Lomond' or just keeping in that range.
Okay. In terms of the business side of your career, you were with Columbia for a time and then MCA.
Yeah, well right after the Claude Thornhill situation, why I found myself pretty much on my own, and by that time also the contract I had with Columbia Artists, although it hadn't terminated,

I think I mentioned earlier that Columbia had to give up its Artist's Bureau so artists like myself were assigned to MCA. MCA was in the business of selling bands and not particularly interested in a solo performer as I was. So for awhile there I just, sort of, sweated out the rest of my contract with MCA booking me in theaters, and I wound up working with different groups. In fact they sent me on a tour, a theater tour, and I left New York, I don't remember the year but I left New York with arrangements for about twenty-two pieces, twenty-two men in the band because there was still a few pit bands left in the theaters. And I traveled from the east coast to the west coast and the farther away from New York I got the smaller the band got. I wound up in Oakland, California with a three-piece band in the pit, and I think it was the Secretary, President and Treasurer of the Local. So, and that's when it got to be a little wearisome being on the road because you never knew what you were going to wind up with. You know, you had to have parts for everybody. It got to be pretty nerve-racking after awhile.
